clue.text: Dry, needing a beer badly? Then use your loaf

indicators.note: something done badly is botched and jumbled, so the letters come out in a muddled order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A thirsty person craving a beer is told to think sensibly instead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Use your loaf' is British slang for 'think', from rhyming slang loaf of bread = head; here the loaf is taken literally.
explanation.definitionFit: Rye bread is commonly baked and sold as a whole loaf made with rye flour.

clue.text: Being sturdy, go off to catch the bus

definitions.note: a participle phrase standing for the adjective

indicators.note: catching something takes hold of it, so the vehicle ends up held inside

blocks.note: food that goes off rots
taken as written

explanation.surface: A strong person heads off to catch the bus.
explanation.definitionFit: Robust describes something strong, solid and hardy, which is what being sturdy amounts to.

clue.text: European Community taking refuge in cake

blocks.note: EC is the abbreviation for European Community
an animal's refuge

explanation.surface: The European bloc hides out in a cake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking refuge in' looks like a container signal, but the refuge supplies letters and they simply follow the bloc's abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: An eclair is a long choux pastry cake filled with cream and topped with chocolate icing.

clue.text: Say no to judge with advantage

blocks.note: a referee judges a game
to be of use is to be an advantage

explanation.surface: Turning down a judge when one has the upper hand.
explanation.definitionFit: To refuse is to decline or reject an offer, which is what saying no does.

clue.text: Committee meeting in heaven without dishonesty

blocks.note: heaven is above us
a board is a committee and also its meeting

explanation.surface: A committee meeting held up in heaven is bound to be honest.
explanation.walkthrough: The blocks are read in the reverse order to the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Above board means open and legitimate, with nothing hidden, like card players' hands kept above the table.

clue.text: Young reporter holds her beautiful child

indicators.note: one thing that holds another keeps it inside, so these letters sit within the outer word

blocks.note: a cub reporter is a novice journalist
taken as written

explanation.surface: A junior journalist cradles a lovely baby, perhaps her own.
explanation.walkthrough: A cub reporter is newspaper jargon for a trainee; 'her' is not a pronoun here but letters to be held.
explanation.definitionFit: A cherub is an angelic figure painted as a chubby infant, so the word describes any sweet, pretty little one.

clue.text: Whoredom causes Henry to go round a lot

indicators.note: going round something encircles it, so the name surrounds the quantity

blocks.note: Harry is the familiar form of Henry
taken as written

explanation.surface: Henry's habit of sleeping around is presented as the cause of prostitution.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry must be turned into its pet form HARRY before it can surround anything.
explanation.definitionFit: Harlotry is the behaviour or trade of a harlot, an old word for prostitute, and so is whoredom.

clue.text: Stop being bloody soft!

blocks.note: blood is red
light as in gentle, soft

explanation.surface: An exasperated plea: quit being so ridiculously feeble!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloody' is a British intensifier meaning 'damned' in the surface, but here it means blood-coloured.
explanation.definitionFit: A red light is the traffic signal that orders vehicles to halt, so it means the command to stop.

clue.text: Not known in cafe, then put out penniless

indicators.note: one item placed in another sits inside it
put out suggests disturbed and displaced, so those letters are thrown out of order
then shows what comes next in the sequence of parts

blocks.note: a bar serving snacks
n.k. is the abbreviation for not known
taken as written

explanation.surface: A stranger in a cafe is thrown out because he has no money.
explanation.walkthrough: NK, short for 'not known', goes into BAR; then PUT is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A bankrupt person or firm cannot pay debts, so is effectively without any money at all.

clue.text: Amphibian exposes speech hindrance behind centre

indicators.note: placing one part behind another fixes their order, with the hindrance coming second

blocks.note: the bull is the centre of a dartboard or target
a frog in the throat makes one hoarse

explanation.surface: A frog-like creature reveals it has a stammer behind some central matter.
explanation.definitionFit: A bullfrog is a large North American frog, an amphibian known for its deep booming call.

clue.text: Poet found in waterless hole

blocks.note: without water
a den is a lair or hole

explanation.surface: A poet is discovered living in a parched burrow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Found in' looks like a container signal but merely links definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: John Dryden was the seventeenth-century English Poet Laureate who wrote Absalom and Achitophel.

clue.text: After a second, playwright embraces small old maid

indicators.note: to embrace is to hug something within one's arms, so the small piece goes inside the dramatist's name
coming after another part means this assembly follows it in the line

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
Harold Pinter, the English dramatist
S is the abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: Shortly afterwards, a dramatist hugs a slightly built elderly unmarried woman.
explanation.walkthrough: PINTER holds S to give PINSTER, which follows S for second.
explanation.definitionFit: An old maid is a dated term for a woman who never married, which is exactly what spinster traditionally means.

clue.text: Mimic joins company at the pier

blocks.note: CO is the abbreviation for company
taken as written

explanation.surface: An impressionist signs up with a theatre troupe performing at the seaside pier.
explanation.definitionFit: A copier is one who imitates or reproduces others, the noun sense of someone who mimics.

clue.text: Does he give a guarantee when dressed in black?

definitions.text: Does he give a guarantee when dressed in black?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone who makes a solemn promise or pledge
setter's reading: the funeral director, traditionally in black, whose title also suggests a person giving a pledge

explanation.walkthrough: An undertaking is a promise, so the job title sounds like 'one who promises'; the black clothes point to funerals.
explanation.definitionFit: A funeral director, traditionally dressed in mourning black, arranges burials, and the title punningly suggests making promises.

clue.text: Crook and son bound to be open all hours, perhaps?

blocks.note: a crook is a bend, as is a corner
S is the abbreviation for son
to bound is to leap or hop

explanation.surface: A criminal and his boy are sure to be working round the clock.
explanation.walkthrough: Open All Hours was a BBC sitcom set in a corner shop; such neighbourhood stores in Britain stay open late. 'Crook' means a bend, not a villain.
explanation.definitionFit: A corner shop is a small local grocery that famously keeps long trading hours, as in the sitcom.

clue.text: Compost getting covered up

blocks.note: first meaning: manure or fertiliser spread over soil
second meaning: putting clothes on

explanation.walkthrough: A top dressing is a layer of fertiliser spread on the ground; the second sense is putting on clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a fertiliser layer applied to soil and the act of putting on clothes.

clue.text: Partisan could be an ambitious person

indicators.note: could be suggests the word may turn into something else, its letters reformed

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A political supporter might turn out to be a careerist.
explanation.definitionFit: An aspirant aspires to rise or achieve some goal, making them someone with ambition.

clue.text: No 1 tin soldier standing up, firing

indicators.note: in a down clue, standing up means the whole run reads from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: taken as written
the Roman numeral for one
taken as written
a GI is an American soldier

explanation.surface: The top tin soldier stays upright when the guns go off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No 1' looks like 'number one' but splits into NO and I.
explanation.definitionFit: Ignition is the act of setting fuel alight, as in firing an engine or a charge.

clue.text: Ground for growing red oranges, maybe

definitions.text: Ground for growing red oranges, maybe
definitions.note: the whole clue describes the answer, with 'Ground' also doing the shuffle

indicators.note: something ground is crushed and broken up, so the letters are reduced and rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A plot of land for raising crimson citrus fruit, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground' reads as a noun for land, but it also signals the shuffle. The 'maybe' admits that the red flowers grown there are roses, not oranges.
explanation.definitionFit: A rose garden is a plot of ground set aside for growing roses, which may well be red or orange.

clue.text: Look for Bill in a lazy way, with sourness

blocks.note: AC, for account, is a bill
doing nothing in a lazy fashion

explanation.surface: Someone is told to hunt for a bill unhurriedly, and grumpily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Look for' is the instruction to find a word for 'Bill'; AC is short for account.
explanation.definitionFit: Acidly means in a sharp, biting manner, the way a sour or caustic remark is made.

clue.text: White man's in white robe and in love

blocks.note: an alb is a white vestment worn by priests
in taken as written, then love as O, a nil score in tennis

explanation.surface: A pale man in a white robe has fallen in love.
explanation.walkthrough: An albino lacks skin pigment, so is literally white.
explanation.definitionFit: An albino has no pigment in skin and hair, so appears strikingly pale and white.

clue.text: Neither Orville nor Wilbur is wrong, we hear

definitions.note: each brother is a member of the family that built the first aeroplane

indicators.note: what we hear is the spoken sound, so the word is spelt differently from how it is said

blocks.note: neither of them is wrong, so both are correct

explanation.surface: Neither of the famous aviation brothers made a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'Neither' does double duty: neither brother is wrong means each is correct.
explanation.definitionFit: Orville and Wilbur were the Wright brothers, so each of them bears the family surname.

clue.text: Demon alcohol?

blocks.note: first meaning: a supernatural being or ghost
second meaning: strong distilled liquor such as gin or whisky

explanation.walkthrough: The surface evokes the old temperance phrase 'demon drink'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both an incorporeal being such as a ghost or demon, and distilled liquor like whisky.

clue.text: Scrupulous person wraps a pound in an adhesive label

indicators.note: wrapping something encloses it, so the label goes around the money

blocks.note: a gummed label
L, from Latin libra, is the abbreviation for a pound

explanation.surface: A careful person sticks a gummed price tag round a pound coin.
explanation.walkthrough: STICKER is split around L.
explanation.definitionFit: A stickler insists on exactness and correct procedure, so is someone scrupulous about details.

clue.text: Type nearly all of it, Alice

indicators.note: nearly all of a word means it falls just short, losing its final letter

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, then cut short

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to type up almost everything Alice says.
explanation.walkthrough: ALICE loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Italic is a style of type with letters that slope to the right, used for emphasis.

clue.text: Uncontrolled road movement means finally fooling around

indicators.note: finally points to the very end of the word before it, keeping only its closing letter

blocks.note: the last letter of means
kidding is joking or fooling around

explanation.surface: A careless driver's antics end up as a loss of control on the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Means' looks like a link word, but supplies its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Skidding is a vehicle sliding on the road surface after its wheels lose grip, a movement the driver cannot steer.

clue.text: Restriction of free speech about money is a punishment

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it, so the restriction goes round the money

blocks.note: a gag silences someone
tin is old slang for money

explanation.surface: Censoring talk about finances is presented as a form of penalty.
explanation.walkthrough: Gating is the British school or college punishment of confining a student to the premises.
explanation.definitionFit: Being gated, kept within the grounds as a penalty, is a traditional disciplinary sanction in schools and colleges.

clue.text: Pupil in drab jacket, being wrong age to cry

indicators.note: letters that are wrong are out of place, so they need rearranging

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A schoolchild in a dull uniform is too old to be weeping.
explanation.walkthrough: Greycoat schools, such as the Grey Coat Hospital in London, were charity schools named after their pupils' grey uniforms.
explanation.definitionFit: A greycoat was a charity-school child dressed in a dull grey uniform, so literally a scholar in a drab coat.
